statement_source_and_scope_match: CB17 Eq. (1.1) and Definition 3.1 give the exact polynomial formulation; BE13 §11 independently uses the same degree inequality and delta in (0,1). Nonzero constants are explicit to avoid an undefined zero-polynomial degree. No unproved equality with a finite-order optimum is imposed.
proposed_statement_text:
Let $\mathcal H$ be the set of nonzero real polynomials whose roots all have strictly negative real part; nonzero constant polynomials belong to $\mathcal H$. Define

$$
\mathcal D=\left\{\delta\in(0,1):\quad
\begin{array}{l}
\text{there exist }x,y\in\mathcal H\text{ with }\deg y\le\deg x,\\[2pt]
(s^2-2\delta s+1)x(s)+(s^2-1)y(s)\in\mathcal H
\end{array}\right\}.
$$

Determine the exact value of

$$
\delta_* = \sup\mathcal D.
$$

The polynomial degrees are arbitrary finite integers, and coefficients are arbitrary real numbers. Stability is strict. The question asks for the sharp threshold over all degrees, with matching feasibility and impossibility arguments, rather than an optimum within a prescribed controller family. It is a supremum: the endpoint need not be attained by a pair of strictly stable polynomials.
applied_significance: For the plant $G_\delta(s)=(s^2-1)/(s^2-2\delta s+1)$, the quotient $y/x$ represents a proper, stable, minimum-phase linear time-invariant controller. The displayed combination is its closed-loop characteristic polynomial under negative feedback. The problem tests stabilization limits when an unstable pole approaches an unstable zero, a difficulty that also arises in engineering control design.
